title: COP31 struggles to reach deal with parties at odds over fossil fuels
html:
Activists unsatisfied with the proposed draft at COP31 hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall. (Reuters: Umit Bektas)

In short:

COP31 climate talks in Türkiye are continuing as nations struggle to reach an agreement.

The most contested issue is the language around fossil fuels.

What's next?

A session to begin approving the final deal is scheduled to start at 5pm AEDT.

Global climate talks are continuing for a second day past deadline as a disagreement over explicit mentions of fossil fuels continues to divide countries and threatens to derail a final deal.

Nations have struggled to reconcile differences at the annual negotiations, against a backdrop of soaring energy prices, geopolitical tensions stemming from the war in Iran, and increasingly dangerous impacts of extreme weather.

Türkiye is hosting this year's conference, but Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen is the lead negotiator.

Chris Bowen is at the helm of climate negotiations in Antalya. (Reuters: Umit Bektas)

The organisers released a final deal early on Sunday morning, Antalya time, which keeps a call to electrify the global economy but makes no mention of fossil fuels despite a fierce backlash when they were stripped from an earlier proposal.

The burning of coal, oil and gas is the key driver of global warming, and in the lead-up to these talks, the UN announced the world would likely pass the most ambitious 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial temperatures.

"We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon," COP31 president Murat Kurum said.

"Outside of this hall there are people who are living with the effects of climate change," Kurum told negotiators early on Sunday. "The children, the parents are waiting for this."

Advisers surround Murat Kurum as nations struggle to reconcile differences. (Reuters: Murad Sezer)

Instead, the revised proposal by COP31 alludes to a 2023 agreement to shift from fossil fuels but stops short of naming them explicitly.

Head of political strategy at 350.org Andreas Sieber said last year's COP30 president Brazil had released a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, but this year's presidencies "chose to ignore it".

"The final draft confirms what has become increasingly clear throughout COP31; an indefensible failure of leadership by the Turkish and Australian presidencies," he said.

"They found room for a 2035 carbon capture target, yet struck the transition away from fossil fuels from the text and launched no initiative to take it forward.

"Brazil showed that such leadership was possible."

The latest draft retains a proposal to boost the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 alongside efforts to expand the use of "clean energy".

Facing pressure over fossil fuels, Türkiye and Australia had pitched "electrification" as a way to cut heat-trapping emissions and bolster energy security.

The push to replace technologies that burn fossil fuels directly, such as diesel cars and gas heating, with electric alternatives will cut emissions due to efficiency, but critics say they should be powered by renewable energy to reduce emissions further.

The text also calls for "accelerating" carbon capture and storage, a contentious technology championed by the fossil fuel industry. Its inclusion in a previous draft faced staunch opposition from countries that point to its high cost and meagre record in cutting emissions.

Director of the International Climate Politics Hub, Cat Abreu, said a focus on carbon capture and storage "came out of nowhere".

"It has been parachuted into COP31 by fossil fuel interests and must not be allowed to make it into a final global agreement," she said.

Because they require consensus from nearly 200 delegations, COP talks regularly run past planned deadlines, but only one so far has ended without an agreement.

Delegations have until 0300 GMT to raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled at 0600 GMT (5pm AEDT) to begin approving it.

AFP/AP
summary: The Antalya text keeps a call to electrify economies and accelerate carbon capture; delegations had until 0300 GMT to object before an approval session.
